summary: D480 applies quality assurance to every phase of the software life cycle, and students report that it's graded on two written performance-assessment tasks built on one bug-ticket scenario: a software design plan for the fix, then a quality assurance plan for testing it. Both 2025 posters passed both tasks on the first try, and one reports about 8 hours of work and 10 days including grading, with tips such as labeling requirements for traceability and answering in the rubric's own words.
author: Dorian Acosta

assessment.type: Performance assessment: two written tasks, a software design plan and a quality assurance plan, evaluator-graded
assessment.format: 2 tasks (reported) · Task 1 design plan + Task 2 QA plan for the same bug-fix scenario · rubric-graded, no exam
details: The tasks (reported): in general terms (your task page has the exact requirements), both tasks work from one scenario built around a bug ticket for an existing application. Task 1 plans the fix as a software design plan, from the problem and its requirements to the design and how the work gets done. Task 2 plans how you'll verify the fix as a quality assurance plan, with quality metrics, test cases and a test order, so it builds directly on Task 1.

Effort and grading: a Jan 2025 passer reports about 8 hours of work and 10 days including grading, with both tasks passing first time, and the Jul 2025 poster also passed both first try. Evaluators grade each task against its rubric and return it with feedback when an item falls short (WGU's general PA process). One student whose Task 2 came back met with an instructor and learned the summary needed more detail on deliverables, tools, languages and methodology.
Catalog status: D480 is 3 CU in term 8 of both BSCS 202412 and 202611 and is also part of B.S. Software Engineering (202610).
tips: Label every item for traceability (BR1, FR1, NFR1, TC1) and reuse the same labels from Task 1 through Task 2, so each test case points back to a requirement.
Use the rubric's own words in headings and sentences so the evaluator finds every item.
Keep it small and concrete: a problem statement of about a paragraph, as many items as your rubric asks for and no more, and every item tied to the ticket.
Give every non-functional requirement a number, a unit and a condition, then reuse that number as its Task 2 quality metric and pass criterion.
For a bug fix, both 2025 passers chose Agile. Compare it with the other methodologies on the same criteria, and justify the choice with the fix's size, urgency and need for fast feedback.
List test environments short of production: the Jan 2025 passer used local, development, test and user acceptance testing (UAT) environments.
In Task 2's summary, restate Task 1's deliverables, tools, languages and methodology; that's what one returned summary lacked.
Fix Grammarly's correctness suggestions before submitting. The Jan 2025 passer says references are needed only if you used sources.

competencies: Course planning: discuss your course planning tool report with your instructor and create your personalized course plan together (listed first in the program guidebook).
The learner defines plans for development tasks and environments based on desired quality outcomes.
The learner determines the impact of business requirements on software design patterns and software systems.
The learner identifies goals and potential roadblocks as part of software development plans.
The learner recommends tools and services to address functional and non-functional testing outcomes.

topics.title: Software quality: QA, QC and testing
topics.eli5: Quality assurance is making sure the kitchen follows good recipes and hygiene rules, and testing is tasting the dish before it leaves the kitchen.
topics.detail: D480 applies a QA focus to every phase of the life cycle, not just a test phase at the end. Quality assurance is process-oriented and preventive: standards, checklists, process audits and plans that make defects less likely. Quality control is product-oriented and detective: activities, testing among them, that find defects in what was built. Testing either executes the software (dynamic testing) or examines work products without running them (static testing, such as reviews and static analysis) to find defects and build confidence. In ISTQB's terms, a person makes an error (a mistake), which can leave a defect (a fault or bug) in code or a document, and executing a defect can cause a failure that users see. Finding problems early, by reviewing requirements and designs and testing as the code is written (often called shifting left), costs far less than finding them in production, which is why a QA plan starts from the requirements. The course description gives usability special weight because users ultimately decide whether an application succeeds.
points: QA prevents (process) · QC detects (product) · testing, dynamic or static (reviews, static analysis), is the main form of QC
Error (human mistake) → defect (in the work product) → failure (visible wrong behavior)
Verification asks whether you built it right, against the specification; validation asks whether you built the right thing for users
A bug ticket is a failure report: the design plan finds and fixes the defect, and the QA plan proves it's gone without breaking anything else

topics.title: Problem statements, business requirements and scope for a fix
topics.eli5: Before fixing a leak, you write down which pipe it is, what it should do, what it's doing now and which nearby pipes you're deliberately not touching.
topics.detail: A design plan opens by framing the ticket. A good problem statement says which application, users and feature are involved, what should happen, and what actually happens, how often and with what impact, in plain language and without proposing the solution yet; the Jul 2025 passer needed only about 140 words. Business requirements state what the business needs from the feature, such as customers completing checkout or staff seeing accurate stock levels, and it helps to say how the current app falls short of each. In-scope action items are the concrete pieces of work the fix includes, each mapped to the business requirement it serves. Out-of-scope items are related things the ticket might tempt you to do but won't, such as redesigning the whole page, adding new features or fixing an unrelated bug noticed nearby. A clear scope keeps a fix small, testable and quick to ship, and it later tells you what to test and what to leave out.
points: Problem statement checklist: who is affected · what should happen · what happens instead · how often · why it matters
Map every action item to a business requirement; an action item with no requirement behind it is probably scope creep
Good out-of-scope items are plausible: they relate to the ticket but not to the fix
Write business requirements from the business's side, as outcomes, not as technical tasks

topics.title: Functional and non-functional requirements with measurable targets
topics.eli5: A functional requirement is what the button does, and a non-functional requirement is how fast, how safely and for whom it does it, written as a number you can check.
topics.detail: Functional requirements describe behavior, and for a bug fix they read like acceptance criteria for each action item: specific, testable statements of what the system shall do. The Given-When-Then format from behavior-driven development keeps them testable: Given a starting context, When an action or event happens, Then an observable outcome follows. Non-functional requirements set quality targets drawn from ISO/IEC 25010:2023's characteristics, such as performance efficiency, reliability, security, interaction capability (called usability in the 2011 edition), compatibility and maintainability, and each needs a metric, a target value and the condition it applies under. For web performance, Google's Core Web Vitals give ready-made thresholds, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads: Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint within 200 milliseconds and Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1 or less. Accessibility targets can cite WCAG 2.2 level AA, and security targets can cite the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS 5.0, published May 2025). Label each requirement (FR1, NFR1) and trace it to its business requirement.
points: Functional: Given a signed-in customer with items in the cart, When they apply a valid coupon, Then the discounted total appears and the coupon shows as applied
Non-functional: the order-history page loads within 2 seconds for 95% of requests with 500 concurrent users
Vague words to replace with numbers: fast, secure, reliable, user-friendly, scalable
Reuse the same numbers in Task 2: a non-functional requirement's target becomes its quality metric and its pass criterion

topics.title: Software behavior and software structure
topics.eli5: Behavior is how the system acts (press this and that happens), and structure is how it's built (which parts exist and what each part is responsible for).
topics.detail: A design plan describes the fixed system from both views. Behavior describes inputs and events, the responses they should produce and the constraints around them: for example, when a user submits a form with an empty required field, the form shows an inline error, doesn't submit and announces the error to screen readers. State, timing and error handling belong here too, including what happens on invalid input, timeouts or a lost connection. UML's behavior diagrams express these views: use case diagrams (actors and goals), activity diagrams (workflows), sequence diagrams (messages between objects over time) and state machine diagrams (states and the events that change them). Structure describes the static organization: the modules or components, each one's purpose and responsibilities, and how they depend on each other. A common way to present it is by layer, such as the user interface, the controllers or services that hold business logic, and the data-access layer and database, with UML structure diagrams such as class, component, package and deployment diagrams. High cohesion within modules and low coupling between them keep a fix contained to the modules that own the problem.
points: Behavior entry pattern: trigger (input or event) → expected response → constraints (time, validation, security)
Structure entry pattern: module → purpose → components → responsibilities
Name the same modules in your structure section that your behavior steps pass through
Single responsibility: each module should have one reason to change

topics.title: Design patterns and how requirements shape design
topics.eli5: Design patterns are proven blueprints for common problems, like a standard staircase design, so you don't have to invent a new one every time you need to reach another floor.
topics.detail: One competency asks how business requirements affect design patterns and software systems. A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem. The Gang of Four catalog has 23 of them: five creational patterns for creating objects (Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, Singleton), seven structural patterns for composing objects (Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy) and eleven behavioral patterns for how objects interact (Chain of Responsibility, Command, Interpreter, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Observer, State, Strategy, Template Method, Visitor). Architectural patterns work at a larger scale, such as layered architecture and Model-View-Controller (MVC), which separates data and rules (model), presentation (view) and input handling (controller). Requirements drive the choice: supporting several interchangeable payment providers points to Strategy, wrapping a third-party API whose interface doesn't match points to Adapter, notifying many parts of the system when an order changes points to Observer, and simplifying access to a tangled legacy subsystem points to Facade. A bug fix should usually respect the patterns already in the codebase rather than introduce new ones, because changing a pattern ripples into every module that depends on it.
points: Strategy: swap interchangeable algorithms at run time, such as shipping-cost rules
Observer: one change notifies many subscribers, such as order-status updates
Adapter: wrap an incompatible interface so your code can use it
Facade: one simple entry point to a complex subsystem
Singleton: exactly one shared instance; use it sparingly, since it adds hidden global state

topics.title: Deliverables, sequencing and roadblocks
topics.eli5: Planning the work is like planning a road trip: list the stops, put them in an order that makes sense, and think ahead about the detours that could slow you down.
topics.detail: A list of deliverables, in order, turns the design into a plan of work. Deliverables are tangible outputs, such as an updated design document, the corrected code, automated tests and a deployed release, each with the steps that produce it, usually design, implement and test. A sequence table orders the deliverables and justifies the order through dependencies: you can't test code that hasn't been written, and an interface should be settled before the code that calls it. A work breakdown structure splits deliverables into smaller tasks, and a finish-to-start dependency means one task must end before the next begins. A competency asks you to identify goals and potential roadblocks, so note what could block each step, such as an unclear root cause, missing test data, no access to an environment, a third-party outage or competing priorities, along with a mitigation for each. Justifications are strongest when they name the dependency or risk that makes the order sensible.
points: A complete sequence row: deliverable · steps · owner · depends on · justification
Typical order for a fix: reproduce and analyze → design the change → implement → unit and integration tests → regression → UAT → release
Roadblock examples: the bug can't be reproduced, no production-like data, a reviewer is unavailable, an API rate limit
Define done for each deliverable, such as all tests passing and the code review approved

topics.title: Development environment and tooling
topics.eli5: The development environment is the workshop: the languages, tools and machines you'll use, chosen because they fit the job and the people doing it.
topics.detail: Describe the development environment and justify each part. List the programming languages and frameworks (matching the existing application, since a fix shouldn't switch stacks), the IDE, version control (Git, with a branch per ticket and pull requests for review), build and dependency tools, issue tracking (such as Jira or GitHub Issues), testing tools and the hosting or deployment target. Continuous integration means merging work into a shared mainline at least daily, with an automated, self-testing build on every push; continuous delivery keeps the product releasable at all times, so releasing is a business decision; and continuous deployment sends every change that passes the pipeline to production automatically. A competency asks you to plan development tasks and environments based on desired quality outcomes, so tie each tool to a quality goal: linting and static analysis to maintainability, automated tests in the pipeline to regression safety, and a staging environment that mirrors production to trustworthy test results. Separate environments, typically local, development, test or QA, staging or UAT, and production, keep unfinished work away from users.
points: Justify by fit: the existing stack, the team's skills, cost, how the tool joins the pipeline, and the quality goal it supports

Feature-branch workflow for a ticket: branch → commits → pull request → automated checks and code review → merge (the GitHub flow pattern; Git Flow is a different model with develop, release and hotfix branches)
Example pairings: Java with Spring Boot in IntelliJ IDEA · TypeScript with React in VS Code · Python with Django in PyCharm
Test in a clone of production, with the same versions, configuration and realistic data, so results carry over

topics.title: Methodologies for a bug fix
topics.eli5: A small, urgent repair doesn't need a year-long master plan; it needs a quick loop of fix, check and ship, with the customer able to see progress.
topics.detail: Choose a methodology and compare it with the alternatives. Waterfall runs requirements, design, implementation, testing and deployment once, in sequence, which suits large fixed-scope projects but is slow and rigid for a small fix. The incremental model delivers working pieces in planned increments; RAD (rapid application development) moves fast through prototypes and heavy user involvement; and continuous development, meaning continuous integration plus continuous delivery or deployment, moves small changes through an automated pipeline so that each one is releasable as soon as it passes (continuous delivery) or goes live automatically (continuous deployment). Agile methods, whether Scrum's sprints or Kanban's continuous flow, suit a bug fix because the work is small, priorities can shift, feedback arrives quickly and each change can be tested and released on its own; both 2025 passers chose Agile. A strong answer states the choice, compares it with the alternatives on the same criteria, and ties each reason to the ticket's size, urgency and risk. Agile and continuous delivery combine well: sprints or a Kanban board plan the work, and the pipeline tests and releases it.
points: Waterfall: one long pass, heavy documentation, late feedback
Incremental: planned slices of functionality, each delivered working
RAD: prototypes and user feedback in short cycles, strongest when the user interface is the main risk
Kanban: pull the ticket when capacity frees up and limit work in progress, which fits a steady stream of fixes
Continuous delivery: always releasable · continuous deployment: every passing change goes live automatically

topics.title: Quality metrics
topics.eli5: Metrics are the scoreboard for quality: numbers that show whether testing was thorough, whether the fix works and whether the system is fast and stable enough.
topics.detail: A QA plan sets quality metrics for the functional and non-functional requirements and says why each one matters. A metric needs a definition, a formula or measurement method, a target and a reason. Test and process metrics include requirements coverage (requirements with at least one passing test divided by all requirements in scope), test pass rate (passed tests divided by executed tests), code coverage (statement coverage counts executed statements and branch coverage counts exercised branches, including both outcomes of every decision, and 100% statement coverage doesn't guarantee 100% branch coverage), defect density (defects per thousand lines of code or per function point), defect removal efficiency (defects found before release divided by all defects found before and after release) and escaped defects (defects found in production). Product metrics map to non-functional requirements: response time at a percentile such as p95, error rate (failed requests divided by total requests), availability (uptime divided by total time), mean time between failures (MTBF), mean time to recovery (MTTR), Core Web Vitals for web pages, WCAG 2.2 AA conformance for accessibility, and usability scores such as the System Usability Scale (SUS), a 10-item questionnaire scored from 0 to 100 on which about 68 is average. Tie each metric to a requirement label and state the threshold that counts as a pass.
points: Functional examples: 100% of in-scope functional requirements covered by a passing test · no open critical or high-severity defects at release
Non-functional examples: p95 response time ≤ 2 s · error rate under 1% · availability ≥ 99.9% · every WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA success criterion met on the changed pages
Why a metric matters: the risk it reveals and the decision it supports, such as release or don't release
Defect removal efficiency = pre-release defects ÷ (pre-release + post-release defects) × 100%

topics.title: Test levels and test types
topics.eli5: Testing happens at different zoom levels, from one tiny part up to the whole system in users' hands, and it asks different questions: does it work, is it fast, is it secure, is it easy to use?
topics.detail: The ISTQB Foundation syllabus separates test levels, which describe scope, from test types, which describe the quality being checked. CTFL v4.0 names five levels: component (unit) testing checks one component in isolation, often with test doubles; component integration testing checks the interfaces and interactions between components; system testing checks the whole system against its requirements in a production-like environment; system integration testing checks the interfaces with other systems and external services; and acceptance testing confirms the system meets users' business needs, with user acceptance testing (UAT) as one of its main forms. Many teams shorten the list to unit, integration, system and acceptance. Types: functional testing checks what the system does; non-functional testing checks how well it does it (performance, load, stress, security, usability, accessibility, compatibility); white-box testing is based on the internal structure; and black-box testing is based on the specification. After a fix, confirmation testing (re-testing) checks that the original failure is gone, regression testing checks that the change didn't break anything that used to work, and a smoke test is a quick check that a build is stable enough to test further. The test pyramid advises many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and only a handful of slow end-to-end tests. The course description names test plans, test cases, and unit, integration, regression and usability tests, so expect to choose among them and justify your choices.
points: Level = scope (component → component integration → system → system integration → acceptance) · type = the quality being checked (functional, performance, security, usability …)
Performance family: load (expected peak), stress (beyond the peak until it breaks), spike (sudden jumps), endurance or soak (sustained load for hours)
Usability testing: real users attempt realistic tasks while you measure success rate, time on task and errors
Confirmation testing proves the bug is fixed; regression testing proves nothing else broke

topics.title: Writing test cases
topics.eli5: A test case is a mini-experiment: a clear setup, an exact action, a specific input and a prediction you check.
topics.detail: Each test case should trace to one requirement (FR1, NFR2), name a test type that fits it (unit, integration, system, regression, performance, usability or acceptance), give concrete sample input, and state an expected result that's observable and clearly passes or fails. Black-box design techniques choose efficient inputs: equivalence partitioning (one representative from each class of inputs that should behave the same), boundary value analysis (values at and just beyond each edge), decision tables (every combination of conditions and the action each requires) and state transition testing (valid and invalid moves between states). Include negative tests that feed invalid input and expect a specific, graceful error, plus a regression test for the scenario that originally failed.
points: Row checklist: ID · requirement label · test type · sample input · an expected result that clearly passes or fails
Typical owners: developers for unit tests, QA analysts for integration, system and regression tests, product owners or end users for UAT
Expected result = an observable output, message or state change, never "works correctly"
Turn the bug's reproduction steps into the first test case: it should fail before the fix and pass after it

topics.title: Test sequence, environments and tools
topics.eli5: You check the bricks before the wall and the wall before the house, and you rehearse in practice rooms before anything reaches the real stage.
topics.detail: Order the tests and justify the order. The usual order follows dependencies: unit tests first (fast, cheap and close to the code), then integration tests on the interfaces the fix touches, then system and non-functional tests in a production-like environment, then regression tests across the affected areas, and finally user acceptance testing before release. Each stage has entry criteria (what must be true to start, such as a build that passed its unit tests) and exit criteria (what must be true to finish, such as no open critical defects), and justifying the order means pointing to those dependencies and to the rising cost of finding problems late. Environments progress from local to development, test or QA, and staging or UAT, and the Jan 2025 passer kept production out of the test plan. A competency asks you to recommend tools and services for functional and non-functional testing: unit frameworks (JUnit for Java, pytest for Python, Jest for JavaScript), UI automation (Selenium, Playwright or Cypress), API testing (Postman), performance testing (Apache JMeter or k6), web audits (Lighthouse for performance and accessibility, axe for accessibility), security scanning (ZAP), static analysis (SonarQube), CI services (GitHub Actions or Jenkins) and defect tracking (Jira). Recommend each one for a stated testing outcome, not just by name.
points: Sequence: unit → integration → system and non-functional → regression → UAT → release
Entry criteria start a stage and exit criteria end it; both make the order defensible
Run the unit and regression suites automatically in CI on every pull request
Pick tools that fit the stack: JUnit for a Spring app, Jest for a React front end, k6 or JMeter for load

practice.q: Which activity is quality assurance rather than quality control?
choices: Running the full regression suite on the release candidate before it ships
Defining a code review checklist and a branching policy for every change
Logging a defect found during system testing, with the steps to reproduce it
Measuring the page's load time in the staging environment against its target
practice.answer: Defining a code review checklist and a branching policy for every change
practice.why: Quality assurance is process-oriented and preventive: it sets up standards and practices, such as a code review checklist and a branching policy that every change must follow, so defects are less likely. Running the regression suite, logging a defect and measuring load time all examine the product to detect problems, which is quality control, and testing is one form of it.

practice.q: A developer misreads a requirement and writes a wrong comparison, and customers then see the wrong total at checkout. In ISTQB terms, which part of this story is the failure?
choices: The developer misreading the requirement
The wrong comparison in the code
The bug ticket that reports the problem
The wrong total that customers see
practice.answer: The wrong total that customers see
practice.why: A failure is the visible deviation from expected behavior when the software runs, here the wrong total customers see at checkout. The misreading is the error (a human mistake), and the wrong comparison is the defect it left in the code. The ticket is a defect report that describes the failure; it isn't the failure itself.

practice.q: Which is the best-written non-functional requirement?
choices: Product search shall return results within 2 seconds for 95% of queries with 500 concurrent users.
Product search should be fast and reliable for every customer, even during busy sale periods.
Users shall be able to search products by name and category from the search bar on every page.
Product search shall use a database index on the product name and category columns.
practice.answer: Product search shall return results within 2 seconds for 95% of queries with 500 concurrent users.
practice.why: It names a metric (response time), a target (2 seconds at the 95th percentile) and a condition (500 concurrent users), so a performance test can pass or fail it. "Fast and reliable" can't be measured, searching by name and category is functional behavior, and requiring an index prescribes a design choice instead of stating the quality the business needs.

practice.q: In a Given-When-Then acceptance criterion, what belongs in the Then step?
choices: The starting state of the system
The user's action or triggering event
An observable outcome the test can check
The database tables the code updates
practice.answer: An observable outcome the test can check
practice.why: Given sets the context, When describes the action or event, and Then states the expected result, which should be observable from outside the system, such as a message, a changed total or a new list entry. Internal details like database tables belong in the implementation and its unit tests, not in an acceptance criterion.

practice.q: Which statement belongs in the software structure section rather than the software behavior section?
choices: When a user submits an empty required field, the form shows an inline error and doesn't submit.
If the payment service doesn't answer within 10 seconds, the order is saved as pending and the user is told.
After three failed sign-in attempts, the account locks for 15 minutes.
The CartService module calculates totals and reads prices through the PricingRepository.
practice.answer: The CartService module calculates totals and reads prices through the PricingRepository.
practice.why: Structure describes the parts of the system, their responsibilities and their dependencies, which is what the CartService statement does: it names a module, what it's responsible for and the PricingRepository it depends on for current prices. The other three describe behavior: an input or event, the system's response and the constraints around it (validation, a timeout, a lockout rule).

practice.q: The business requires checkout to support several payment providers, with more added later, without changing the checkout code each time. Which design pattern fits best?
choices: Singleton
Strategy
Observer
Memento
practice.why: Strategy puts interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, so checkout calls a payment strategy and new providers plug in as new implementations; an Adapter often wraps each provider's own API to fit that interface. Singleton guarantees a single instance, Observer notifies subscribers when something changes, and Memento saves and restores an object's state, and none of these addresses swappable providers.

practice.q: For a single, well-understood bug fix that must ship quickly and be checked with the product owner, which approach is the best fit?
choices: Waterfall, with requirements, design and test documents signed off at the end of each phase
The spiral model, with a formal risk analysis and a new prototype in every loop
RAD, with several rounds of throwaway prototypes reviewed in user workshops
Agile, with a short sprint or Kanban flow backed by continuous integration
practice.answer: Agile, with a short sprint or Kanban flow backed by continuous integration
practice.why: A small fix benefits from short feedback loops, quick review with the product owner and independent testing and release, which is what Agile and CI provide. Waterfall's phase sign-offs slow a small change down, the spiral model's risk loops are meant for large, high-risk projects, and RAD's prototyping helps when the user interface is uncertain, not when the bug is well understood.

practice.q: What distinguishes continuous deployment from continuous delivery?
choices: Continuous deployment releases every passing change automatically; continuous delivery keeps the product releasable, and people decide when to release.
Continuous deployment means merging code into the shared mainline at least daily; continuous delivery means a scheduled release to production once a month.
Continuous delivery releases every passing change automatically; continuous deployment keeps the product releasable, and people decide when to release.
There's no difference; the two names mean the same thing.
practice.answer: Continuous deployment releases every passing change automatically; continuous delivery keeps the product releasable, and people decide when to release.
practice.why: Merging into a shared mainline at least daily, with an automated, self-testing build, is continuous integration, and neither delivery nor deployment means a fixed monthly release. Continuous delivery extends that automation so the product is always ready to release, leaving the release itself as a business decision, and continuous deployment goes one step further by sending every change that passes the automated pipeline to production automatically. The reversed option swaps the two definitions: delivery stops at always releasable, and deployment is the one that releases automatically.

practice.q: Testing finds 45 defects before release, and users report 5 more after release. What is the defect removal efficiency?
practice.why: Defect removal efficiency is the defects removed before release divided by all defects found before and after release: 45 ÷ (45 + 5) = 45 ÷ 50 = 90%. 10% is the share that escaped (5 ÷ 50), and 11% divides the escaped defects by the pre-release count (5 ÷ 45).

practice.q: A function contains one if statement with no else, and your only test makes the condition true. Which statement is correct?
choices: Statement coverage can reach 100%, but branch coverage can't
Branch coverage is 100% because every line ran
Statement coverage is 50% and branch coverage is 100%
Coverage can't be measured for a statement without an else
practice.answer: Statement coverage can reach 100%, but branch coverage can't
practice.why: With the condition true, every statement runs, including the body of the if, so statement coverage can reach 100%. But every line running isn't the same as every branch: the decision has a true and a false outcome, and only the true one was exercised, so branch coverage stays below 100%. Most coverage tools count the two decision outcomes and report 50%; ISTQB CTFL v4.0 also counts unconditional branches, which gives a higher figure. A second test that makes the condition false would cover the implicit else and bring branch coverage to 100%.

practice.q: Which test checks that the fixed checkout module and the payment service exchange data correctly through their interface?
choices: A unit test
An integration test
A usability test
A user acceptance test
practice.why: Integration testing targets the interfaces and interactions between components or systems. A unit test checks one component in isolation, usually with the payment service replaced by a test double; a usability test watches real users attempt tasks; and user acceptance testing confirms the whole system meets users' needs before release.

practice.q: After the fix is merged, you rerun the steps from the original ticket and they now pass. Then you run the existing test suites for checkout, cart and sign-in. What are these two activities?
choices: Confirmation testing, then regression testing
Regression testing, then smoke testing
Unit testing, then acceptance testing
Exploratory testing, then confirmation testing
practice.why: Rerunning the failing scenario to prove the defect is gone is confirmation testing (re-testing). Running the existing suites for nearby features to check that the change broke nothing that used to work is regression testing. Smoke testing is a quick stability check of a build, and exploratory testing is unscripted investigation.

practice.q: Where should user acceptance testing of the fix normally run?
choices: On the developer's own machine, with local test data
In a staging environment that mirrors production
In production, during business hours, with real customers
In the unit-test stage of the CI pipeline, on every commit
practice.answer: In a staging environment that mirrors production
practice.why: UAT needs a production-like environment, often called staging or the UAT environment, with the same versions, configuration and realistic data, so users judge the real experience without risking live customers. A developer's machine isn't representative, testing in production exposes users to unverified changes (and the Jan 2025 passer kept production out of the test plan), and the unit-test stage checks components, not user acceptance.

practice.q: Which test sequence is easiest to justify for the fix?
choices: UAT → regression → system → integration → unit
Regression → unit → UAT → integration → system
System → UAT → unit → integration → regression
Unit → integration → system → regression → UAT
practice.why: Each stage depends on the one before it: components should work alone before you test how they connect, the connected system before you check it end to end and for regressions, and the whole system before users spend time on acceptance. Starting with UAT, system tests or regression, before the fix is unit tested, finds defects late, when they cost the most to fix.

practice.q: Which tool best matches the testing outcome "confirm the page stays under a 2-second response time with 500 simultaneous users"?
choices: JMeter or k6
JUnit or pytest
axe or WAVE
Git or Subversion
practice.why: Apache JMeter and k6 generate simulated concurrent users and report response-time percentiles, which is exactly a load-testing outcome. JUnit and pytest run unit tests for Java and Python code, axe and WAVE check web pages for accessibility problems, and Git and Subversion are version control systems, not testing tools.

pitfalls: Untraceable items. Requirements without labels, or labels that change between tasks, make it hard to show that each test covers a requirement. Label everything (BR1, FR1, NFR1, TC1) and reuse the labels in Task 2.
Non-functional requirements without numbers. "The page should load quickly" can't become a quality metric or a test. Give each one a metric, a target and a condition.
A problem statement that wanders or jumps to the solution. Keep it to who is affected, what should happen and what happens instead; the Jul 2025 passer needed about 140 words.

Scope items that don't connect. In-scope action items should map to business requirements, and out-of-scope items should relate to the ticket without being part of the fix. Unrelated filler weakens both lists.

Mixing behavior and structure. Events and responses belong in behavior, while modules and responsibilities belong in structure. Listing components under behavior, or rules under structure, misses both items.
Describing Agile without comparing. Naming a methodology isn't a justification. Compare it with the alternatives on the same criteria and tie the choice to the fix's size, urgency and risk.
A thin Task 2 summary. One returned summary lacked detail on deliverables, tools, languages and methodology. Restate them from Task 1.

Incomplete test case rows. Every row needs a requirement label, a test type, concrete sample input and an expected result that clearly passes or fails. An expected result of "it works" isn't checkable.
Testing in production, or a sequence with no reasons. Put tests in local, development, test and UAT environments, and justify the order with its dependencies and entry or exit criteria.

caveats: The task outline here is a general summary from two 2025 posts, not from WGU, whose task directions and rubrics are behind the login. Details may have changed since, so follow your rubric wherever it differs from this guide.

This guide deliberately doesn't describe the scenario's application or its bug; it teaches the concepts each section needs. Your scenario's details decide what your requirements, modules and test cases contain.
Reddit couldn't be opened directly for this research, so post details come from condensed notes, and dates are approximate (converted from Reddit's relative timestamps).
The tools, metrics and targets named here are common industry examples, not WGU requirements. Choose what fits your scenario's stack and justify it.
The practice questions are original concept checks written for this guide. The PA has no multiple-choice items; the questions test the ideas the two plans rely on.
